---
title: "Equilibria and stability: one-variable models"
subtitle: "Otto & Day, chapter 5, with PracticalCAS"
engine: julia
---

A model in one variable either gives the rate of change, `dn/dt = f(n)`, or
the next value, `n(t+1) = f(n(t))`. Its equilibria are where nothing changes:
`f(n) = 0` in continuous time and `f(n) = n` in discrete time. An equilibrium
`n̂` is locally stable when small perturbations shrink. That depends on the
slope `λ = f′(n̂)`: in continuous time it needs `λ < 0`, and in discrete time
`-1 < λ < 1`. In discrete time a negative `λ` also means the approach
oscillates.

```{julia}
using PracticalCAS
@syms n::nonneg r::positive K::positive R::positive
```

## Exponential and logistic growth

With an intrinsic rate `ρ` of unknown sign, the only equilibrium of
exponential growth is `n = 0`. It is stable exactly when the population
declines (`ρ < 0`).

```{julia}
@syms ρ
expo = ode(n => ρ * n)
stability(expo)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(only(stability(expo)).condition, ρ < 0)
```

Logistic growth has equilibria `0` and `K`. With `r > 0` the sign engine
decides both verdicts without further input.

```{julia}
logistic = ode(n => r * n * (1 - n / K))
equilibria(logistic)
```

```{julia}
stability(logistic)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
st = Dict(only(values(s.point)) => s for s in stability(logistic))
@assert st[toterm(0)].verdict === :unstable && st[K].verdict === :stable
@assert st[K].eigenvalues == [-r]
```

## Discrete logistic, Ricker and Beverton–Holt

In discrete time the carrying capacity can lose stability. For the discrete
logistic `n + r n (1 - n/K)` the slope at `K` is `1 - r`.

```{julia}
dlog = recurrence(n => n + r * n * (1 - n / K))
sK = stability(dlog, Dict(n => K))
sK.eigenvalues, sK.condition
```

The approach is oscillatory when the eigenvalue is negative, that is when
`r > 1`:

```{julia}
simplify(sK.eigenvalues[1] < 0)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(sK.eigenvalues[1], 1 - r)
@assert isequiv(sK.condition, r < 2)
@assert isequiv(simplify(sK.eigenvalues[1] < 0), r > 1)
```

The Ricker model behaves the same way near `K`. The Beverton–Holt model never
overshoots: its slope at `K` is `1/R`, between 0 and 1 whenever `R > 1`.

```{julia}
ricker = recurrence(n => n * exp(r * (1 - n / K)))
equilibria(ricker), stability(ricker, Dict(n => K)).condition
```

```{julia}
bh = recurrence(n => R * n / (1 + (R - 1) * n / K))
stability(bh, Dict(n => K)).eigenvalues
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert Set(e[n] for e in equilibria(ricker)) == Set([toterm(0), K])
@assert isequiv(stability(ricker, Dict(n => K)).condition, r < 2)
@assert isequiv(only(stability(bh, Dict(n => K)).eigenvalues), 1 / R)
```

## Haploid selection

Allele `A` at frequency `p` has fitness `WA`, allele `a` has fitness `Wa`. One
generation of selection gives `p′ = p WA / (p WA + (1 - p) Wa)`.

```{julia}
@syms p::[0, 1] WA::positive Wa::positive
hap = recurrence(p => p * WA / (p * WA + (1 - p) * Wa))
[(e[p], stability(hap, e).condition) for e in equilibria(hap)]
```

So `p = 1` (fixation of `A`) is stable when `A` is fitter. The continuous-time
version `dp/dt = s p (1 - p)` gives the same picture with the selection
coefficient `s`.

```{julia}
#| include: false
hs = Dict(e[p] => stability(hap, e).condition for e in equilibria(hap))
@assert isequiv(hs[toterm(1)], Wa < WA)
@assert isequiv(hs[toterm(0)], WA < Wa)
```

```{julia}
@syms s
hapc = ode(p => s * p * (1 - p))
[(e[p], stability(hapc, e).condition) for e in equilibria(hapc)]
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
hc = Dict(e[p] => stability(hapc, e).condition for e in equilibria(hapc))
@assert isequiv(hc[toterm(1)], s > 0) && isequiv(hc[toterm(0)], s < 0)
```

## Diploid selection

With genotype fitnesses `WAA`, `WAa`, `Waa` and random mating, the allele
frequency after selection is `(p² WAA + p q WAa) / W̄`, where `W̄` is the mean
fitness. Besides `p = 0` and `p = 1` there is a polymorphic equilibrium.

```{julia}
@syms WAA::positive WAa::positive Waa::positive
q = 1 - p
Wbar = p^2 * WAA + 2p * q * WAa + q^2 * Waa
dip = recurrence(p => (p^2 * WAA + p * q * WAa) / Wbar)
eqs = equilibria(dip)
```

```{julia}
p̂ = only(e[p] for e in eqs if !(e[p] isa Num))
```

It is stable under heterozygote advantage and unstable under heterozygote
disadvantage. Here are both cases with numbers:

```{julia}
st = stability(dip, Dict(p => p̂))
over = (WAA => 9 // 10, WAa => 1, Waa => 8 // 10)
under = (WAA => 11 // 10, WAa => 1, Waa => 12 // 10)
decide(subs(st.condition, over...)), decide(subs(st.condition, under...))
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(p̂, (WAa - Waa) / (2WAa - WAA - Waa))
@assert decide(subs(st.condition, over...)) === true
@assert decide(subs(st.condition, under...)) === false
```

The fixation equilibrium `p = 1` is stable exactly when `AA` is fitter than
`Aa`:

```{julia}
stability(dip, Dict(p => 1)).condition
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(stability(dip, Dict(p => 1)).condition, WAa < WAA)
```
